triage.name: Prediabetes
triage.reason: Common asymptomatic metabolic condition found on screening; students can reach it through risk-factor history and labs, with counseling implications.

demographics: About 1 in 3 US adults has prediabetes, and most are unaware of it
Prevalence rises with age and is higher in African American, Hispanic/Latino, American Indian, Alaska Native, Asian American, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander adults
More common in people with lower income and less access to healthy food and safe places to exercise

risk_factors.text: Overweight or obesity (especially increased waist circumference)
History of gestational diabetes or delivering a baby over 9 lb
Metabolic syndrome (high blood pressure, high triglycerides, low HDL, central obesity)
History of cardiovascular disease or stroke
Non-white race or ethnicity (higher risk at lower BMI)
Sleep apnea or chronic sleep deprivation

comorbidities: Prior stroke or transient ischemic attack
family_history: Type 2 diabetes in a parent or sibling
Gestational diabetes in the patient's mother
social_history: Limited access to affordable healthy food

chief_complaints.text: I actually feel fine — my doctor said my blood sugar was a little high
I've been told I'm at risk for diabetes
I've noticed dark, velvety patches on my neck and under my arms
I'm tired all the time and I've put on some weight

hpi.onset: Insidious; develops silently over years and is usually found on routine screening rather than reported by the patient
hpi.duration: Present for months to years before detection
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive insulin resistance; glucose drifts upward over time and may eventually cross into type 2 diabetes, but many patients remain stable for years
hpi.location: Systemic metabolic condition; no focal location
hpi.quality: Asymptomatic in most patients; when symptoms occur they are vague and nonspecific
hpi.timing: Constant background risk; no episodic pattern

associated_symptoms.text: No symptoms at all — found on screening labs
Darkened, velvety skin in the armpits or on the back of the neck (acanthosis nigricans)
Small skin tags in the same areas

pertinent_negatives: Numbness, tingling or burning in the feet
Ketoacidosis or hospitalization for high blood sugar

positives.text: Feeling tired or low on energy

argues_against: Weight loss with high blood sugar suggests overt diabetes rather than prediabetes

positives.text: Gradual weight gain around the middle

argues_against: Thyroid disease or other endocrine cause of the metabolic picture

negatives: Numbness or tingling in the feet
Burning pain in the hands or feet
argues_against: Diabetic peripheral neuropathy, which points to established diabetes

positives.text: Skin tags on the neck or under the arms

argues_against: Established diabetes with poor wound healing

atypical.how_it_differs: Prediabetes is increasingly found in children and teens with obesity, but it is usually picked up on screening rather than reported; acanthosis nigricans may be the only visible clue.
Very common and often found alongside multiple other chronic conditions and medications; symptoms are even less likely to be reported, and fatigue may be attributed to age or other illnesses.
Glucose levels are interpreted with pregnancy-specific thresholds; a woman may have had gestational diabetes in a prior pregnancy and now have prediabetes outside of pregnancy.
missing_classic_features: Standard non-pregnant A1C and fasting glucose cutoffs

atypical.how_it_differs: Patients with severe obesity may have normal fasting glucose but abnormal 2-hour glucose on an oral glucose tolerance test, so a normal A1C or fasting glucose does not fully exclude prediabetes.

general.mild: Well-appearing, comfortable, no distress; often overweight or obese with central adiposity
general.moderate: Well-appearing but with more marked central obesity and features of metabolic syndrome
general.severe: Well-appearing but with severe obesity and multiple metabolic syndrome features; still no acute distress
general.critical: Not applicable — prediabetes does not produce a critical general appearance

findings.maneuver: Inspect the back and sides of the neck
Inspect the neck and axillae for small raised growths
Measure waist circumference at the top of the iliac crest, or assess central adiposity on inspection
Measure height and weight and calculate BMI
findings.finding: BMI in the overweight or obese range

findings.maneuver: Measure blood pressure in both arms with an appropriately sized cuff
findings.finding: Elevated blood pressure, often in the hypertensive range

findings.maneuver: Inspect the feet and test vibration, pinprick and monofilament sensation
findings.finding: No ulcers, no loss of protective sensation, intact distal pulses

findings.maneuver: Check visual acuity and, if trained, perform a fundoscopic exam
findings.finding: Normal visual acuity; no retinopathy on fundoscopy

findings.maneuver: Test deep tendon reflexes and distal sensation in the hands and feet
Inspect the skin for ulcers, boils or non-healing wounds
findings.finding: No chronic wounds or recurrent skin infections

labs.caveat: 5.7–6.4% is the prediabetes range; 6.5% or higher on two occasions indicates diabetes. Reflects average glucose over about 3 months and can be falsely low in anemia, hemoglobin variants, recent transfusion, or chronic kidney disease.
Fasting plasma glucose of 100–125 mg/dL is impaired fasting glucose; requires at least 8 hours of fasting. A single value is not enough — confirm with a repeat test or a second modality.
Low HDL is part of the dyslipidemia that clusters with insulin resistance; values below the sex-specific cutoff support metabolic syndrome.
Fasting triglycerides of 150 mg/dL or higher are a metabolic syndrome criterion and commonly accompany insulin resistance.
Mild elevation suggests nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, which frequently coexists with prediabetes; consider hepatic steatosis workup if persistently elevated.
Usually rises with ALT in fatty liver disease; an AST/ALT ratio above 1 can suggest more advanced fibrosis.
Urine glucose is usually negative in prediabetes because the renal threshold is not exceeded; a positive result suggests glucose has risen above roughly 180 mg/dL and points toward overt diabetes.

findings.text: No hemodynamically significant stenosis; intima-media thickness may be mildly increased
Coronary calcification may be present and helps refine cardiovascular risk

initial.why: First-line test for prediabetes; 5.7–6.4% establishes the diagnosis without fasting
Fasting plasma glucose of 100–125 mg/dL is an alternative diagnostic criterion; requires 8-hour fast
Assesses the dyslipidemia that clusters with insulin resistance and guides cardiovascular risk reduction
Baseline renal function and electrolytes; also provides a fasting glucose if drawn fasting
Thyroid disease can cause fatigue and weight change that mimic the metabolic picture
initial.only_if: symptoms suggest thyroid dysfunction or the picture is atypical

supporting.why: Screens for nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, which commonly accompanies prediabetes
Paired with ALT to assess for fatty liver disease
Checks for glucose or protein in the urine; usually normal in prediabetes
supporting.only_if: osmotic symptoms or suspicion of kidney involvement

not_indicated.why: Not routinely needed for prediabetes; anemia can affect A1C interpretation but is not part of the diagnostic workup
No role unless acute coronary syndrome is suspected
No role in the evaluation of prediabetes
Not part of prediabetes workup; pregnancy changes glucose thresholds and should be tested when pregnancy is possible and diabetes screening is being interpreted
Not routinely indicated for prediabetes alone; reserved for suspected carotid disease or specific risk stratification
Not routinely indicated; may be considered in selected patients for cardiovascular risk refinement

decision_points: Confirm an abnormal A1C or fasting glucose on a separate day or with a second modality before labeling prediabetes
A1C may be unreliable in anemia, hemoglobin variants, recent transfusion, or chronic kidney disease — use fasting glucose or oral glucose tolerance test instead
Screen for prediabetes in adults with overweight/obesity plus one or more risk factors, and in all adults starting at age 35
A normal A1C or fasting glucose does not fully exclude prediabetes in severe obesity; consider 2-hour oral glucose tolerance test

criteria.name: American Diabetes Association prediabetes criteria
criteria.summary: Prediabetes is defined by any of the following: fasting plasma glucose 100–125 mg/dL (impaired fasting glucose), 2-hour plasma glucose 140–199 mg/dL during a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (impaired glucose tolerance), or A1C 5.7–6.4%. Values should be confirmed on a separate day unless the diagnosis is clinically clear.

differential.name: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
differential.why_considered: Same underlying insulin resistance and risk factors; the only difference is how far glucose has risen, so a single borderline value can be misclassified.
differential.trigger: A1C 6.5% or higher, fasting glucose 126 mg/dL or higher, or any osmotic symptoms

history: Polyuria, polydipsia or unintentional weight loss
Longer duration of risk factors such as obesity and family history
exam: Findings of established complications such as diminished foot sensation or foot ulcers
labs: A1C 6.5% or higher, or fasting plasma glucose 126 mg/dL or higher, confirmed on a second occasion
Random glucose 200 mg/dL or higher with classic symptoms

differential.name: Type 1 diabetes mellitus
differential.why_considered: Can present with mild hyperglycemia in adults, especially slowly progressive forms, and shares the finding of elevated glucose.
differential.trigger: Lean or younger patient, rapid symptom onset, or ketones present

history: Weight loss despite normal or increased appetite
Rapid onset of thirst and urination over weeks
Personal or family history of autoimmune disease
exam: Thin body habitus without central obesity
Signs of dehydration or ketosis such as deep respirations
labs: Positive diabetes autoantibodies (GAD65, islet cell, insulin, IA-2, ZnT8)

differential.name: Medication-induced hyperglycemia
differential.why_considered: Several common drugs raise glucose and can produce a prediabetes-range A1C or fasting glucose without true underlying insulin resistance.

history: Recent start or dose increase of a glucocorticoid, antipsychotic, thiazide, beta blocker, protease inhibitor, tacrolimus, niacin or valproic acid
Temporal link between the drug and the abnormal glucose
labs: Glucose improves after the offending drug is stopped or reduced
Normal glucose before the medication was started

differential.name: Stress hyperglycemia
differential.why_considered: Acute illness, surgery, trauma or infection can transiently raise glucose into the prediabetes range.

history: Recent acute illness, hospitalization, surgery or infection
labs: Glucose normalizes after the acute illness resolves
A1C is normal or near normal, reflecting only a short period of hyperglycemia

differential.name: Hypothyroidism
differential.why_considered: Causes fatigue and weight gain that overlap with the vague symptoms sometimes attributed to prediabetes, and can modestly affect glucose and lipid levels.

history: Cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair thinning
exam: Bradycardia, delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes, diffuse hair loss, periorbital puffiness
labs: Elevated TSH with low free T4
Glucose and A1C are usually normal or only mildly abnormal

differential.name: Metabolic syndrome without dysglycemia
differential.why_considered: Shares central obesity, hypertension and dyslipidemia with prediabetes and is often present at the same time, so the metabolic picture can be mistaken for prediabetes alone.

history: Central weight gain, hypertension and dyslipidemia without known glucose abnormality
exam: Increased waist circumference and elevated blood pressure
labs: A1C below 5.7% and fasting glucose below 100 mg/dL

differential.name: Cushing syndrome
differential.why_considered: Cortisol excess causes central obesity, glucose intolerance and hypertension that can look like prediabetes with metabolic syndrome.

history: Progressive central weight gain, easy bruising, proximal muscle weakness, mood changes
exam: Moon facies, dorsocervical fat pad, purple abdominal striae, proximal myopathy
labs: Elevated late-night salivary cortisol, abnormal 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test, or elevated 24-hour urine free cortisol

differential.name: Polycystic ovary syndrome
differential.why_considered: Insulin resistance is central to PCOS, and many affected women have prediabetes-range glucose; the hormonal features can dominate the picture.

history: Irregular or absent menses, hirsutism, acne, infertility
exam: Hirsutism, acne, male-pattern hair loss, acanthosis nigricans
labs: Elevated total or free testosterone, elevated LH to FSH ratio
Glucose may be normal or in the prediabetes range
imaging: Ovarian morphology with multiple small follicles on pelvic ultrasound

severity.mild: A1C 5.7–6.0% or fasting glucose 100–110 mg/dL; no symptoms; weight and blood pressure near goal
severity.moderate: A1C 5.9–6.2% or fasting glucose 108–118 mg/dL; central obesity, hypertension or dyslipidemia present; lifestyle change not yet established
severity.severe: A1C 6.1–6.4% or fasting glucose 115–125 mg/dL; multiple metabolic syndrome features; high short-term risk of progressing to type 2 diabetes

red_flags.finding: A1C 6.5% or higher, or fasting glucose 126 mg/dL or higher, confirmed
red_flags.meaning: This is diabetes, not prediabetes; treatment targets change

red_flags.finding: Polyuria, polydipsia or unintentional weight loss
red_flags.meaning: Osmotic symptoms suggest overt diabetes and warrant prompt evaluation
Meets the threshold for diabetes when symptoms are present

red_flags.finding: Ketones in blood or urine with hyperglycemia
red_flags.meaning: Suggests type 1 diabetes or ketosis-prone diabetes rather than prediabetes

red_flags.finding: Foot ulcer, loss of protective sensation, or persistent blurred vision
red_flags.meaning: Points to established diabetes with complications, not prediabetes

complications.name: Progression to type 2 diabetes
clues: Rising A1C or fasting glucose over serial visits
Continued weight gain or physical inactivity
Strong family history of type 2 diabetes

complications.name: Cardiovascular disease and stroke
clues: Chest pain or exertional shortness of breath
Prior transient ischemic attack or stroke

complications.name: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease
clues: Central obesity and metabolic syndrome features

complications.name: Chronic kidney disease
clues: Reduced eGFR or albuminuria on screening
Long-standing hypertension or diabetes risk factors

complications.name: Diabetic retinopathy
clues: Usually only after progression to overt diabetes

complications.name: Peripheral neuropathy
clues: Numbness, tingling or burning in the feet
Loss of protective sensation on monofilament testing

special_populations.differences: Prediabetes is increasingly found in children and teens with obesity; screening is based on BMI percentile and risk factors, and acanthosis nigricans may be the only visible clue. Lifestyle counseling involves the whole family.

Very common and often accompanied by multiple chronic conditions and medications that raise glucose; fatigue may be attributed to age or other illnesses, and A1C can be affected by anemia or kidney disease.

Glucose is interpreted with pregnancy-specific thresholds; a history of gestational diabetes markedly increases the risk of later prediabetes and type 2 diabetes, so postpartum screening is important.

Patients with severe obesity may have a normal A1C or fasting glucose but abnormal 2-hour glucose on an oral glucose tolerance test, so a normal A1C or fasting glucose does not fully exclude prediabetes.
A1C may be falsely low in advanced chronic kidney disease due to anemia and shortened red cell survival; fasting glucose or oral glucose tolerance testing is preferred.

key_questions.question: What brings you in today — have you noticed any symptoms, or was this found on a routine test?
key_questions.looking_for: Usually no symptoms; abnormal glucose found on screening. Symptoms like thirst, urination or weight loss point to overt diabetes.

key_questions.question: Have you been more thirsty, urinating more often, or losing weight without trying?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in prediabetes; if present, suggests diabetes rather than prediabetes.

key_questions.question: Have you noticed any dark, velvety patches on your neck or under your arms, or small skin tags?
key_questions.looking_for: Acanthosis nigricans and skin tags — visible clues of insulin resistance.

key_questions.question: Has your weight changed recently, and how would you describe your usual diet and activity level?
key_questions.looking_for: Weight gain, central adiposity, sedentary habits and high-calorie diet — modifiable drivers.

key_questions.question: Do you have high blood pressure, high cholesterol, or has a doctor ever mentioned metabolic syndrome?
key_questions.looking_for: Clustered cardiometabolic risk factors that accompany insulin resistance.

key_questions.question: Have you ever had gestational diabetes, or delivered a baby weighing over 9 pounds?
key_questions.looking_for: Strong risk factor for prediabetes and later type 2 diabetes.

key_questions.question: Has a parent, brother or sister been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes?
key_questions.looking_for: First-degree family history — a strong risk factor.

key_questions.question: Do you have PCOS, sleep apnea, or any history of heart disease or stroke?
key_questions.looking_for: Conditions associated with insulin resistance and higher cardiovascular risk.

key_questions.question: Are you taking any steroids, antipsychotics, thiazide diuretics, beta blockers or other regular medications?
key_questions.looking_for: Drugs that can raise glucose and mimic prediabetes.

key_questions.question: Have you had any numbness, tingling or burning in your feet, or any non-healing wounds?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent in prediabetes; present suggests established diabetes with complications.

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or drink alcohol, and what is your access to healthy food and safe places to exercise?
key_questions.looking_for: Modifiable risk factors and social barriers that shape the counseling plan.

reasoning_points: Most patients are asymptomatic and the condition is found on screening rather than reported symptoms

Risk factors: overweight or obesity with central adiposity, age 45 or older, first-degree relative with type 2 diabetes, physical inactivity, prior gestational diabetes, PCOS, metabolic syndrome, and higher-risk race or ethnicity
A1C of 5.7–6.4% or fasting plasma glucose of 100–125 mg/dL establishes prediabetes; a 2-hour glucose of 140–199 mg/dL on a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test is an alternative criterion
An abnormal result should be confirmed on a separate day or with a second modality before labeling prediabetes
A1C can be unreliable in anemia, hemoglobin variants, recent transfusion or chronic kidney disease — use fasting glucose or oral glucose tolerance testing instead
Absence of osmotic symptoms (polyuria, polydipsia, unintentional weight loss) and absence of complications such as neuropathy, retinopathy or non-healing wounds argues against overt diabetes
A1C 6.5% or higher or fasting glucose 126 mg/dL or higher means diabetes, not prediabetes, and changes management
Prediabetes raises the risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and stroke, so counseling on weight loss, activity and diet is central to the plan

easy: Middle-aged adult with overweight or obesity and a strong family history of type 2 diabetes
No symptoms; abnormal A1C or fasting glucose found on routine screening
Acanthosis nigricans on the neck or axillae
Hypertension and dyslipidemia as part of the metabolic picture
medium: Normal fasting glucose but abnormal 2-hour glucose on oral glucose tolerance testing
A1C in the prediabetes range with a coexisting condition such as PCOS or prior gestational diabetes
Patient taking a medication that raises glucose, such as a glucocorticoid or antipsychotic
Older adult with fatigue and weight gain where hypothyroidism or other causes must be excluded
hard: Severe obesity with a normal A1C and fasting glucose but abnormal oral glucose tolerance test
A1C unreliable due to anemia, hemoglobin variant, recent transfusion or chronic kidney disease
Glucose abnormality that resolves after an acute illness or after stopping an offending medication
Borderline result that could represent early type 2 diabetes rather than prediabetes
Patient with Cushingoid features where cortisol excess is the underlying cause
